messages.subject: Negative Binomial version of the two species static binomial N-mixture model and directional interactions
parts:
Hi All,

I am working on a two species static binomial N-mixture model (AHEM2 Chapter 8.5.2) and was wondering if anyone has ran with model with a negative binomial distribution, instead of the Poisson distribution noted in the text?

I am using repeat-transect electrofishing data and it is likely that the individuals captured do not occur independently of each other nor randomly.

Any resources or code for this would be greatly appreciated!

All the best,

Jacqueline

Best regards,
Frederik

messages.subject: Re: Negative Binomial version of the two species static binomial N-mixture model and directional interactions
parts:
Hi Jacqui, Frederik,

personally I like the Poisson-lognormal (PLN) better than the NegBin, because I understand it better. But in terms of the inferences they are typically pretty similar. If you want to fit the NegBin in JAGS, you will want a re-parameterization in terms of the mean. We have BUGS code for this in Section 7.6 (pages 336-337) in the AHM1 book and if you don't have access to that, then you should be able to find that code on the book website.

Just beware of unreasonably high abundance estimates under the NegBin (and presumably also the PLN), which may sometimes arise.

Best regards  --- Marc

Thanks Frederik and Marc for your notes. 

Given that PLN is more straight forward and returns similar results to NegBin, I've attempted to use PLN in my code. However, I keep running into the error below. Any thoughts?

" Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) :
  3 nodes produced errors; first error: RUNTIME ERROR:
Compilation error on line 24.
Attempt to redefine node tau[1] "



# Specify model in BUGS language
cat(file = "Nmix2.txt", "
model {
  # Model for Brook Trout (BKTR): the 'dominant' species
  # Priors for intercepts and coefficients
 
  mean.lambdaK ~ dunif(0, 35)
  beta0K <- log(mean.lambdaK)
  alpha0K <- logit(mean.pK)
  mean.pK ~ dunif(0,1)
 
  beta1K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta2K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta3K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta4K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta5K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta6K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta7K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta8K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta9K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)

  alpha1K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  alpha2K ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
 
  tau ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1) # Excess-Poisson variation (precision)
  sigma <- sqrt(1 / tau)


  # Likelihood for BKTR ('dominant')
  # Ecological model
  for (i in 1:nsites){
    NK[i] ~ dpois(lambdaK[i])
    eta[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau)
    log(lambdaK[i]) <- beta0K + beta1K * dist_ms[i] + beta2K * water_temp[i] + beta3K * elev[i] + beta4K * pool[i] +
    beta5K * riffle[i] + beta6K * depth_avg[i] + beta7K * lwd[i] + beta8K * timber_area[i] + beta9K * rip_area[i]  +
    eta[i]
   
    # Observation model
    for (j in 1:nreps){
      CK[i,j] ~ dbin(pK[i,j], NK[i])
      logit(pK[i,j]) <- alpha0K + alpha1K * SECONDS[i,j] + alpha2K * WET_WIDTH[i,j]
    }
  }
 
 
  # Model for Bull Trout (BLTR): the 'subordinate' sp.
  # Priors for intercepts and coefficients
 
  mean.lambdaL ~ dunif(0, 55)
  beta0L <- log(mean.lambdaL)
  beta1L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta2L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta3L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta4L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta5L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta6L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta7L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta8L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  beta9L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
 
  alpha0L <- logit(mean.pL)
  mean.pL ~ dunif(0,1)
  alpha1L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  alpha2L ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
 
  gamma0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1) # These are the 'interaction coefficients' !
  gamma1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma3 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma4 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma5 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma6 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma7 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma8 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  gamma9 ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)

  tau ~ dgamma(0.1,0.1) # Excess-Poisson variation (precision)
  sigma <- sqrt(1 / tau)

 
  # Likelihood for BLTR ('subordinate')
  # Ecological model
  for (i in 1:nsites){
    NL[i] ~ dpois(lambdaL[i])
    eta[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau)
    lambdaL[i] <- exp(beta0L + beta1L * dist_ms[i] + beta2L * water_temp[i] + beta3L * elev[i] + beta4L * pool[i] + beta5L * riffle[i] +
    beta6L * depth_avg[i] + beta7L * lwd[i] + beta8L * timber_area[i] + beta9L * rip_area[i] + gamma0 * NK[i] + gamma1 * dist_ms[i] * NK[i] +
    gamma2 * water_temp[i] * NK[i] + gamma3 * elev[i] * NK[i] + gamma4 * pool[i] * NK[i] + gamma5 * riffle[i] * NK[i] + gamma6 * depth_avg[i] * NK[i] +
    gamma7 * lwd[i] * NK[i] + gamma8 * timber_area[i] * NK[i] + gamma9 * rip_area[i] * NK[i] + eta[i])
   
    # Observation model
    for (j in 1:nreps){
      CL[i,j] ~ dbin(pL[i,j], NL[i])
      logit(pL[i,j]) <- alpha0L + alpha1L * SECONDS[i,j] + alpha2L * WET_WIDTH[i,j]
    }
  }
}
")


# Initial values
Nst <- rep(20, nsites)
inits <- function() list(NK = Nst, NL = Nst)

# Parameters monitored
params <- c('mean.lambdaK', 'beta1K', 'beta2K','beta3K','beta4K','beta5K','beta6K','beta7K','beta8K','beta9K', 'mean.pK', 'alpha1K',
            'alpha2K', 'mean.lambdaL', 'beta1L', 'beta2L', 'beta3L', 'beta4L', 'beta5L', 'beta6L', 'beta7L', 'beta8L', 'beta9L','mean.pL',
            'alpha1L', 'alpha2L', 'gamma0', 'gamma1', 'gamma2', 'gamma3', 'gamma4', 'gamma5', 'gamma6', 'gamma7', 'gamma8', 'gamma9', 'sigma')

# MCMC settings
na <- 5000 ; nc <- 3 ; ni <- 300000 ; nb <- 100200 ; nt <- 200

# Call JAGS
out2 <- jags(abun.bltr.bktr, inits=NULL, params, "Nmix2.txt", n.adapt = na,
             n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, parallel = TRUE)

 
Best,

Jacquie

Hi Jacqui, Frederik,

personally I like the Poisson-lognormal (PLN) better than the NegBin, because I understand it better. But in terms of the inferences they are typically pretty similar. If you want to fit the NegBin in JAGS, you will want a re-parameterization in terms of the mean. We have BUGS code for this in Section 7.6 (pages 336-337) in the AHM1 book and if you don't have access to that, then you should be able to find that code on the book website.

Just beware of unreasonably high abundance estimates under the NegBin (and presumably also the PLN), which may sometimes arise.

Best regards  --- Marc

etaSite[i] + etaStream[Stream[i]]
       etaSite[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.eta.site)
}
for(i in 1:nstream){
  etaStream[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.eta.stream)
}

Here, Stream is an vector of length 'nsites' which contains the stream membership of each site.

Dear Jacquie,

yes, there are many approaches to model selection and no agreement among statisticians about which is best.
  • You may not do model selection at all, but just build a single big model that has all potentially interesting terms in it and then present that. This isn't even as shocking as it may sound as first; for instance Gelman seems to have liked this approach for a long time.
  • Sequentially removing terms (= "backwards elimination") is an antique method that is still done since it's so easy.
  • Exploring variants of a single model ("iterating a single model") is something in between that has been advocated recently by ver Hoef, see  https://wildlife.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.891
  • Hooten and Hobbs (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/14-0661.1) advocate model selection based on the predictive ability of a model. You can assess that in-sample (for the same data that you fit your model to) or out-of-sample (to new data). The latter is the gold standard, but more expensive (e.g., need more data)
  • Short-cuts are to estimate the predictive ability in-sample, e.g., as in AIC. Among the Bayesian counterparts of AIC, the WAIC seems to be the preferred information criterion recently. For instance, Jeff Doser's spOccupancy package gives the WAIC. You can code this up in JAGS for yourself, or alternatively use NIMBLE, which has a function to compute it for any (?) model
  • Cross-validation, including leave-one-out (LOO)-CV, is also a common method to assess the predictive ability of a model. An information criterion based on LOO is provided in Ken Kellner's ubms package. For models fit in Stan, there's the loo R package which allows computation of a LOO criterion from a single model fit. In principle, one can also apply that package with MCMC output from other software, but needs the log-predictive density of the data. This is not something that JAGS provides so if you wanted to stay with JAGS, you'd have to try to code that up yourself.
  • For Bayesian model selection in occupancy models, this is a relevant paper: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/15-1471.1
Best regards  --- Marc

On Thu, 17 Feb 2022 at 20:16, Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

Dear Jacquie,

yes, there are many approaches to model selection and no agreement among statisticians about which is best.
  • You may not do model selection at all, but just build a single big model that has all potentially interesting terms in it and then present that. This isn't even as shocking as it may sound as first; for instance Gelman seems to have liked this approach for a long time.
  • Sequentially removing terms (= "backwards elimination") is an antique method that is still done since it's so easy.
  • Exploring variants of a single model ("iterating a single model") is something in between that has been advocated recently by ver Hoef, see  https://wildlife.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.891
  • Hooten and Hobbs (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/14-0661.1) advocate model selection based on the predictive ability of a model. You can assess that in-sample (for the same data that you fit your model to) or out-of-sample (to new data). The latter is the gold standard, but more expensive (e.g., need more data)
  • Short-cuts are to estimate the predictive ability in-sample, e.g., as in AIC. Among the Bayesian counterparts of AIC, the WAIC seems to be the preferred information criterion recently. For instance, Jeff Doser's spOccupancy package gives the WAIC. You can code this up in JAGS for yourself, or alternatively use NIMBLE, which has a function to compute it for any (?) model
  • Cross-validation, including leave-one-out (LOO)-CV, is also a common method to assess the predictive ability of a model. An information criterion based on LOO is provided in Ken Kellner's ubms package. For models fit in Stan, there's the loo R package which allows computation of a LOO criterion from a single model fit. In principle, one can also apply that package with MCMC output from other software, but needs the log-predictive density of the data. This is not something that JAGS provides so if you wanted to stay with JAGS, you'd have to try to code that up yourself.
  • For Bayesian model selection in occupancy models, this is a relevant paper: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/15-1471.1
Best regards  --- Marc

  • Short-cuts are to estimate the predictive ability in-sample, e.g., as in AIC. Among the Bayesian counterparts of AIC, the WAIC seems to be the preferred information criterion recently. For instance, Jeff Doser's spOccupancy package gives the WAIC. You can code this up in JAGS for yourself, or alternatively use NIMBLE, which has a function to compute it for any (?) model
  • Cross-validation, including leave-one-out (LOO)-CV, is also a common method to assess the predictive ability of a model. An information criterion based on LOO is provided in Ken Kellner's ubms package. For models fit in Stan, there's the loo R package which allows computation of a LOO criterion from a single model fit. In principle, one can also apply that package with MCMC output from other software, but needs the log-predictive density of the data. This is not something that JAGS provides so if you wanted to stay with JAGS, you'd have to try to code that up yourself.
  • For Bayesian model selection in occupancy models, this is a relevant paper: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/15-1471.1
